newsitem.title: USA: Florida high court to rule on stadium bond issue.
newsitem.headline: Florida high court to rule on stadium bond issue.

text.p: Hillsborough County officials and a former Tampa mayor squared off Wednesday over whether the Tampa Sports Authority's $204.5 million bond issue to revamp its stadium to keep a professional football franchise is a deal too sweet for the Florida Supreme Court.

Florida's highest court heard arguments and is expected to rule shortly on whether the city and county broke constitutional bounds by agreeing to revamp Tampa Stadium to keep the Tampa Bay Buccaneers football team from seeking greener pastures.
The NFL team has demanded that an improved stadium be built by January 1 2000, saying otherwise it is free to leave the city for another market.
Last fall, Hillsborough County residents passed a referendum approving the use of bond money for stadium improvements.
Former Tampa Mayor Bill Poe filed suit arguing that the city-financed stadium improvements were unconstitutional. In March a local circuit judge agreed.

Attorneys representing the city argued Wednesday that the team brings in an estimated $3 billion a year into the local economy, a figure that far outweighs any financial gain experienced by the team, known locally as the Bucs.

"Tampa isn't doing anything that other cities' wouldn't do to secure a professional sports franchise. In addition to the financial incentives, an NFL franchise also contributes in non-monetary ways, by giving local residents a hometown team and the Tampa Bay area a public relations boost," said Hillsborough County Attorney Emeline Acton.
"These things are important things for the community...and those are the things that far outweigh what the Buccaneers are getting."

Attorneys for former mayor Bill Poe, however, said the estimated $600 million to be paid by local taxpayers over the next 30 years is not justified and amounts to public support for a profit-seeking private business. The money instead should go for other public uses.
"Under this agreement, none of the Bucs' revenues goes to repay the bonds," said attorney Chris Bentley. "None of it."

In March, Hillsborough circuit judge Sam Pendino ruled that despite the team's economic impact, it was illegal for the city to levy a sales tax increase to refurbish the stadium for the benefit of the team.
Under a proposed lease agreement, the Bucs would receive most of the revenue from non-Bucs events ranging from college football games to tractor pulls.

Last fall, local voters passed a countywide referendum approving a half-cent increase in local sales tax to be used for a host of projects including renovations to the stadium. The tax is also being used to build schools, jails and other public buildings.
